children: Large and creditworthy borrowers don't normally keep real estate lenders awake at night. But a set of keys handed back by Brookfield is a wake-up call. Big investors are pragmatic about walking away from bad apartment deals.
Canadian investor Brookfield manages around $280 billion of real estate. It surrendered the Beaudry apartment building in Los Angeles to its lender Bridge Investment Group this month.

Rents at the Beaudry never rose as much as Brookfield expected, so the building only generated enough income to cover 77% of the mortgage payment in the first six months of this year, according to an analysis by CRED iQ.

Refinancing the Beaudry's $357 million mortgage may have required a fresh cash injection. As apartment values have fallen over the last four years, Brookfield's equity had likely shrunk or been wiped out. It chose to walk away rather than write a check.

Apartments were the hottest real estate trade of 2021 and 2022 when rents were booming and debt was cheap. But they have turned out to be a dud. High interest rates have wiped more than 20% off peak values and a construction boom tipped the apartment market into oversupply, destroying rent growth.

Multifamily apartment rents rose just 0.9% for the nine months through September, compared with the same period of 2025, data from CoStar shows. The delinquency rate on apartment loans in the commercial mortgage backed securities market was 8% in September, based on Trepp data. Only office loans are in worse shape.

Institutional investors such as Brookfield are focused on the bottom line and have responsibilities to their own investors. Leaving cash tied up in an underperforming apartment building can hurt returns and jeopardize future fundraising efforts.

The consequences of handing the keys to the lender are also less severe for an institutional investor than a small owner who would have difficulty accessing capital in the future if they burn their lender. A wealthy family that wants to pass an apartment building down to the next generation may tolerate a few years of low returns rather than trash their credit.

The problem for many investors is that they can't sell the apartments at the price they bought them for. They were hoping that interest rates would have fallen by now. Lower borrowing costs would boost property values and allow them to cash out at a better price.
The waiting game hasn't paid off. After last week's hot inflation data, futures markets are pricing in two to three quarter-point hikes between now and March, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Several apartment buildings bought by large institutional investors in 2021 and 2022 are on watchlists for potentially troubled loans. Another Brookfield property in Brooklyn is only generating enough income to cover 75% of the mortgage payment and the loan matures in three months, CRED IQ data shows.

Insurance giant Guardian Life owns an apartment building in Utah where there is also a big gap between the rent and the mortgage payment. That loan matures next year. Other institutional investors including Goldman Sachs, Blackstone and Lone Star also have properties in a similar situation, but they have more time until maturity.

These loans are current, so lenders and CMBS investors are still getting paid. The owners may have an interest rate hedge in place that covers the shortfall between the rent and the mortgage payments, or they are making up the difference from their own pocket.
A loan maturity is usually the test of whether a borrower is committed to a building.

Many investors who bought apartments in 2021 and 2022 will need to stump up cash to refinance — 57% of maturing apartment debt from deals done in these years will require a cash infusion, according to CRED iQ. If the owner thinks that rent growth will recover, they may decide it is worthwhile putting more money into the building. If not, they could jettison it.

Vacancy rates for apartments are low and plenty of investors still want to buy multifamily properties at the right price. "We expect lenders to experience much lower loss severities on multifamily assets compared to...some particularly bad office loans," says Alex Killick, a managing director at CWCapital Asset Management.
The bad news is that Brookfield is unlikely to be the last big investor to walk away.
